title: The History of Maps
description: A radio series on how maps were made and what they show, from ancient drawings to medieval charts, the politics of a famous projection and digital navigation.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · The first maps
parts.intro: You will hear a radio presenter, Clara, beginning a series about the history of maps.

script.speaker: Clara
script.text: Welcome to Drawn to Scale, a series about the history of maps. Let me begin with a question that sounds easy. What is a map?

script.speaker: Clara
script.text: Most of us would say it's a picture of a place, and so it is. But the oldest maps we know of weren't designed to help anyone find their way. A clay tablet from ancient Mesopotamia, for example, shows a plot of land with its boundaries marked, and its purpose was to settle a legal dispute about who owned what.

script.speaker: Clara
script.text: Other early maps had stranger ambitions. Some, scratched on cave walls or carved in bone, may show the stars, or the places where hunters could expect to find game. We can't be certain. And that uncertainty is revealing. A map is not simply a record of reality; it's a decision about what matters.

script.speaker: Clara
script.text: The ancient Greeks took a more scientific approach. They worked out that the earth is round, and even produced a fairly accurate estimate of its size using nothing more than the shadow of a stick in two different towns. One scholar drew a grid of lines on a map, an idea so useful that we still use it today.

script.speaker: Clara
script.text: Yet for most of history, maps were rare and precious objects, drawn by hand, copied by hand, and often wrong. A map was an act of faith in the person who made it. When the copying introduced errors, they were copied too.

script.speaker: Clara
script.text: In this series, I'll be asking what maps leave out as much as what they put in, because I've come to think that the silences on a map are often the most interesting parts.

parts.title: Part 2 · Medieval maps and sea charts
parts.intro: You will hear Clara talking to a historian, Dr Bell, about maps made in the Middle Ages.

script.speaker: Clara
script.text: Dr Bell, when we picture a medieval map, we tend to imagine something fanciful. Sea monsters, strange peoples at the edges. Is that fair?

script.speaker: Dr Bell
script.text: It's half fair, and I'd like to correct the other half. The large decorated maps in cathedrals were not meant for navigation. They were more like illustrated sermons, with Jerusalem at the centre and the story of the world arranged around it. Asking if they were accurate is a bit like asking if a stained-glass window is accurate.

script.speaker: Clara
script.text: So they weren't failures at geography.

script.speaker: Dr Bell
script.text: Not at all. They succeeded at something else. Meanwhile, sailors had a quite different kind of map. From about the thirteenth century, ship captains in the Mediterranean used charts covered in criss-crossing lines that radiated from compass points. They're astonishingly accurate for coastlines, and they were made by people whose lives depended on them.

script.speaker: Clara
script.text: What did those charts leave out?

script.speaker: Dr Bell
script.text: Almost everything inland. A chart had one job: to get a ship from one harbour to another. Mountain ranges, rivers, even cities beyond sight of the sea, were of little interest. It's a good example of how the purpose of a map decides what it shows.

script.speaker: Clara
script.text: And did the two traditions ever meet?

script.speaker: Dr Bell
script.text: Eventually, yes. As explorers pushed beyond known waters, mapmakers combined the accurate coastlines of the sailors with the scholarly grids of the ancients. It was a slow and untidy marriage, but out of it came the maps of the age of exploration.

script.speaker: Clara
script.text: One last question. Where did all that information come from?

script.speaker: Dr Bell
script.text: Often from sailors' stories. A mapmaker in a warehouse in the capital might never have left the city. He depended on the word of men who had.

parts.title: Part 3 · The politics of projection
parts.intro: You will hear a geographer, Professor Cho, talking about a famous map projection.

script.speaker: Professor Cho
script.text: Every map of the world is a lie, and I mean that quite affectionately. A globe is round, and paper is flat. You cannot flatten a sphere without stretching or tearing something, and the method you choose is called a projection.

script.speaker: Professor Cho
script.text: The most famous was devised in the sixteenth century for sailors. Its great virtue is that a straight line on it gives a constant compass bearing. For a navigator crossing an ocean in a wooden ship, that was a gift. The price was distortion. Places near the poles are stretched enormously, so Greenland looks as large as Africa, when Africa is in fact about fourteen times bigger.

script.speaker: Professor Cho
script.text: For a sailor, that mattered little. The trouble began when the same projection moved from the ship's cabin to the classroom wall. Generations of children grew up believing that Europe was larger than South America, and that the countries of the north were somehow more important.

script.speaker: Professor Cho
script.text: I don't want to exaggerate. Nobody sat down and decided to mislead children. But a picture repeated every day has a quiet influence, and it's reasonable to ask whether the habit of seeing the world that way affected how people thought about it.

script.speaker: Professor Cho
script.text: Alternatives exist. Some preserve the sizes of countries at the cost of distorting their shapes. Others split the world into pieces, like an orange peel. Each has its own weakness, because no projection can do everything.

script.speaker: Professor Cho
script.text: That, to me, is the lesson. There is no neutral map. Whenever you look at one, ask what it was made for, who it was made for, and what it has been forced to sacrifice.

parts.title: Part 4 · Maps in our pockets
parts.intro: You will hear Clara and a technology writer, Sam, discussing digital maps.

script.speaker: Clara
script.text: Sam, almost everyone now has a map in their pocket that knows exactly where they are. Has that changed what a map is?

script.speaker: Sam
script.text: Profoundly. The old paper map was the same for everybody. A digital map is different for each person. It shows the route it thinks you want, the restaurants it thinks you'll like, and it updates itself constantly.

script.speaker: Clara
script.text: That sounds wonderful. I'm sensing a but.

script.speaker: Sam
script.text: There are several. The first is a loss of skill. Studies suggest that people who follow spoken directions remember much less about the route than those who use a paper map. They arrive, but they have no picture of where they've been.

script.speaker: Clara
script.text: I confess that's true of me. I've lived in my town for ten years and I couldn't draw it.

script.speaker: Sam
script.text: The second is more subtle. Behind every digital map is a company deciding what to show. If a business pays to appear, or if a street is judged unsafe by an algorithm, nobody tells you. The map presents itself as neutral, and that's precisely what makes it persuasive.

script.speaker: Clara
script.text: So the old lesson still applies.

script.speaker: Sam
script.text: Absolutely. Every map is an argument. We've simply stopped noticing.

script.speaker: Clara
script.text: Is there a positive side?

script.speaker: Sam
script.text: A big one. Volunteers around the world now draw maps of places that official maps ignore, such as informal settlements, remote villages and roads after a flood. During emergencies, those maps have helped rescuers reach people who didn't officially exist on any chart.

script.speaker: Clara
script.text: A fitting place to end. Maps began as claims about who owns the land, and now they can also be a way of saying, you matter, you're here.
